chapter.title: Descartes and the question of what we can know

cards.body: A man sits by the fire in a winter dressing gown, paper in hand, and decides to doubt every single thing he believes. That's René Descartes in his 1641 *Meditations*, and at the long dinner table he didn't answer the last guest: he swept the table clear and asked how anyone knows anything at all. When the dust settled, **exactly one thing was still standing**.
cards.simpler: Picture a man sitting by the fire in a winter dressing gown, holding a sheet of paper. He decides to doubt every single thing he believes. This is René Descartes, in his 1641 book *Meditations*. Think of a long dinner table where thinkers take turns. Descartes didn't reply to the last guest. He cleared the whole table and asked how anyone knows anything at all. In the end, **exactly one thing was still standing**.

cards.prompt: Descartes sweeps aside everything he believes: what his eyes tell him, his memories, even his maths. One thing survives. Which one?

options.text: That he has a body, sitting in that chair
That he, the one doing the doubting, exists

whyNot.a: That's maths, not the doubter: Descartes imagined a trickster clever enough to fool him even about simple sums.
whyNot.b: That's the senses, not the doubter: a dream can give you a body and a chair that aren't really there.

cards.reteach: Try doubting that you're doubting. You can't, because the doubting is happening right now. And if doubting is happening, someone has to be doing it.

cards.title: Tip out the basket
cards.body:
Descartes compared his method to a basket of apples. If you're afraid a few are rotten, you don't sniff them one by one. You **tip the whole basket out**, and put back only the apples you've checked.

So he ran three rounds of doubt. Round one: your senses sometimes fool you, especially about things that are tiny or far away. Round two: dreams feel completely real while you're in them. Round three, the big one: what if a powerful trickster, an *evil demon*, were faking everything, even the sums in his head?
cards.simpler: Descartes compared his method to a basket of apples. If some may be rotten, you don't sniff them one by one. You **tip the whole basket out** and put back only the ones you've checked. He doubted in three rounds. First, your senses can fool you, especially about tiny or far-away things. Second, dreams feel real while you're in them. Third, what if a powerful trickster, an *evil demon*, faked everything, even sums in his head?

cards.title: The man in the dressing gown
cards.body: Descartes tests his own scene: the fire, the dressing gown, the paper in his hand. Surely that's certain? Round two says no: he has dreamed exactly this scene while actually lying undressed in bed. Round three goes further, because the demon could fake the fire, the paper and his hands. Then he notices something. The demon can fake the paper, but not the person reading it: **someone has to be there to be fooled**.
cards.simpler: Descartes tests his own scene: the fire, the dressing gown, the paper in his hand. Surely that's certain? Round two, the dream test, says no. He has dreamed this exact scene while lying undressed in bed. Round three goes further, since the demon could fake the fire, the paper, even his hands. Then he notices something. The demon can fake the paper, but not the one reading it. **Someone has to be there to be fooled**.

cards.prompt: Your friend Priya, three coffees deep, says: 'What if this whole life is a simulation?' Which reply uses Descartes's move?

options.text: 'Then nothing is certain, not even that you exist.'
'Even if it's fake, something is being fooled. So you, the thinker, exist.'
'Pinch yourself. It feels real, so it is real.'

whyNot.a: That mixes up the doubting with the conclusion: the three rounds end in doubt, but Descartes's whole point is that the doubter survives the doubting.
whyNot.c: That's trusting the senses, which round one already threw out: a simulation could fake the pinch too.

cards.reteach: A simulation is just round three in modern clothes. Descartes would happily agree it might all be fake. What it can't fake is the one having the fake experience.

cards.title: What it proves, and what it doesn't
cards.body:
You'd think doubting everything leaves you with nothing. It leaves you with you. In the *Meditations* he puts it as 'I am, I exist'. In other books he gave it the more famous form, best known in Latin as *cogito, ergo sum*: 'I think, therefore I am'. Here *thinking* means any experience at all, even feeling the fire's heat. It proves only that **a thinking thing exists, right now**. Not your body, not the fire.

That's the turn at the table. Plato and Aristotle argued about the world. Descartes starts inside the mind and has to build a road back out. His road leaned on a good God who wouldn't trick him, and plenty of later guests called that the weakest plank.
cards.simpler: Doubting everything still leaves you. In the *Meditations* he says 'I am, I exist'. In other books he put it the famous way, *cogito, ergo sum*, Latin for 'I think, therefore I am'. Thinking means any experience, even feeling the fire's heat. It proves only that **a thinking thing exists, right now**, not your body, not the fire. Plato and Aristotle argued about the world. Descartes starts inside the mind and must build a road back out. His road relied on a good God who wouldn't trick him, which many later thinkers saw as its weakest plank.

cards.body: At a party, Sam hears 'I think, therefore I am' and nods: 'Great, so my body and this room are real too.' Sam has stretched the line too far. It proves only that a thinker exists: nothing about hands, rooms or the world outside. Descartes needed a whole separate argument to get those back. You can spot the mistake whenever someone uses the line to prove anything beyond the thinker.
cards.simpler: At a party, Sam hears 'I think, therefore I am' and nods: 'Great, so my body and this room are real too.' Sam is stretching the line too far. It proves **only that a thinker exists**. Nothing about hands, rooms or the world outside. Descartes needed a separate argument to get those back. Watch for anyone using the line to prove more than the thinker.

cards.prompt: Strip it down to the bare minimum. What does 'I think, therefore I am' actually prove?

options.text: That your body and the world around you are real
That a thinking thing exists, at least while it's thinking
That thinking harder makes you more real

whyNot.a: That's Sam's party mistake: the line proves the thinker exists, and Descartes needed more steps to get to the body and the world.
whyNot.c: That adds a 'more or less real' scale the line never mentions: it says only that a thinker exists, not how much.

cards.reteach: Picture the basket tipped out: body, fire and maths all on the floor. The one apple left is the bare fact that someone is doing the doubting. Nothing else is back in the basket yet.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Descartes tried to doubt everything, even maths, and found he couldn't doubt that he, the doubter, existed. That moved the long argument from 'what is the world?' to 'what can a mind know for sure?'
cards.simpler: Descartes tried to doubt everything, even maths. One thing he couldn't doubt was that he, the one doing the doubting, existed. That shifted the long conversation from 'what is the world?' to **'what can a mind know for sure?'**

cards.body:
Tonight, pick one thing you're sure of, like 'my phone is on the table'. Put it through Descartes's three rounds: could your eyes be wrong, could you be dreaming, could it all be faked? Notice what's still standing.

Tomorrow: Hume asks why yesterday's sunrise proves anything about tomorrow's.
cards.simpler: Tonight, pick one thing you feel sure of, like 'my phone is on the table'. Run it through Descartes's three rounds of doubt. Could your eyes be wrong? Could you be dreaming? Could it all be faked? Then **notice what's still standing**. Tomorrow, Hume asks why yesterday's sunrise tells us anything about tomorrow's.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain 'I think, therefore I am' and the problem it was built to solve: finding one thing we can know for certain.

dubious_claims: Card 7 suggests Descartes would reject 'I stop existing when I stop thinking', but Meditation II says 'if I ceased entirely to think, I should likewise cease altogether to exist' is possible
Card 1 suggests 'I think, therefore I am' comes from the 1641 fireside book, but the Meditations say 'I am, I exist'. The famous wording is from the Discourse (1637) and the Principles (1644)
Card 3 puts the round-tower example in the first wave of doubt, but Descartes uses it in Meditation VI, near the end of the book
Exercise 2, option c feedback ('giving up one step too early') says what went wrong but doesn't name what the reader confused it with
Exercise 1 feedback uses the 'floor' idea before card 6 introduces it
The 'Tomorrow' teaser is in card 9, but the chapter ends on the 'try' card, so the last line the reader sees isn't the hook for the next chapter
repairedFrom.why: The mistake card says the bus joke misreads Descartes, but in Meditation II Descartes himself says that if he stopped thinking entirely, he might stop existing. So the 'correction' teaches a false point, and the 'which proves' swap test doesn't really check anything.
repairedFrom.fix: Replace the mug joke with a real misreading, like 'so I think, therefore my body and my room are real too', and correct it: the line proves only that a thinker exists, nothing about hands, rooms or the world.
